flashcards.q: What does LEGB stand for and in what order is it searched?
flashcards.a: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in — searched innermost to outermost, stopping at the first scope where the name is found.

flashcards.q: How does Python decide whether a name inside a function is local, and when is that decision made?
flashcards.a: Statically, at compile time, by scanning the entire function body for any assignment to that name. If found anywhere, the name is local for the WHOLE function, even on lines before the assignment.

flashcards.q: Why does `print(x); x += 1` inside a function raise UnboundLocalError instead of reading a global x?
flashcards.a: x += 1 is an assignment, so the compiler marks x local for the entire function body, making the earlier print(x) try to read a local that hasn't been assigned yet.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between global and nonlocal?
flashcards.a: global binds assignments to module scope (and creates the binding if it doesn't exist). nonlocal binds to the nearest enclosing function scope that already defines the name, and raises SyntaxError at compile time if no such scope exists — it never falls back to global.

flashcards.q: Why does `[lambda: i for i in range(3)]` produce three closures that all return 2?
flashcards.a: All three lambdas close over the same cell for loop variable i, not a value captured at creation time. By the time any lambda is called, the loop has finished and the shared cell holds its final value, 2.

flashcards.q: Give two standard fixes for the late-binding closure trap.
flashcards.a: 1) Default argument trick: lambda i=i: i, since defaults are evaluated once at def time. 2) A factory function (def make(i): return lambda: i) that creates a fresh scope/cell per call.

flashcards.q: What is a closure mechanically, in CPython terms?
flashcards.a: A tuple of cell objects (func.__closure__), one per free variable (func.__code__.co_freevars). Each cell is a mutable box shared by reference between the enclosing scope and the nested function.

flashcards.q: Why does `def f(bucket=[]): bucket.append(x)` accumulate values across unrelated calls?
flashcards.a: The default list is evaluated once, at def time, and stored on the function object; every call that doesn't override bucket reuses the same list object.

flashcards.q: Is a class body part of the LEGB chain for a comprehension or method defined inside it?
flashcards.a: No. Class bodies are excluded from the enclosing-scope chain for nested functions and comprehensions, so they can't see other class attributes as bare names (except the outermost comprehension iterable, which is evaluated in the class body before the comprehension's own scope takes over).

flashcards.q: Does a comprehension's loop variable leak into the enclosing scope in Python 3?
flashcards.a: No. Comprehensions have their own scope in Python 3 (unlike Python 2's list comprehensions), so the loop variable is not visible after the comprehension ends.

flashcards.q: Does PEP 709 (Python 3.12 comprehension inlining) change comprehension scoping rules?
flashcards.a: No, it's a performance optimization (avoids a full nested function call per comprehension); the comprehension's own scope and non-leaking loop variable behavior are preserved by design.

flashcards.q: Why is `Thread(target=lambda: worker(i))` inside a loop dangerous, and what's the fix?
flashcards.a: All spawned threads' lambdas close over the same shared cell for i, so most/all threads can end up calling worker with the loop's final value, non-deterministically depending on scheduling. Fix: Thread(target=worker, args=(i,)), which copies the current value at call time instead of sharing a cell.
